### Summary ###

Solution found with answer: \boxed{\{0,1,3\}

### Detailed Solution ###

Summary**

**a. Verdict**  
I have found a complete solution.  
The admissible values of \(k\) are  

\[
\boxed{\{0,1,3\}}\qquad\text{for every integer }n\ge 3 .
\]

In particular, \(k=2\) and every \(k\ge 4\) are impossible.

**b. Method Sketch**  

1.  Write the required set of lattice points as  

    \[
    S_{n}= \{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{2}\mid a+b\le n+1\}.
    \]

2.  Show that \(k=0\) (all horizontal lines) and \(k=1\) (all horizontal lines except one sunny line through the unique uncovered point) are always realizable.

3.  Prove that \(k=2\) is never possible: after using \(n-2\) non‑sunny lines (e.g. the horizontal lines \(y=1,\dots ,y=n-2\)) the three points  

    \[
    (1,n),\;(1,n-1),\;(2,n-1)
    \]

    remain uncovered, and any line through two of them is non‑sunny; consequently two sunny lines cannot cover all three.

4.  Reduce the problem for \(k\ge 3\) to the case \(k=n\): if we can cover the triangle \(S_{k}\) with exactly \(k\) sunny lines, then for any \(n\ge k\) we cover the lower part of \(S_{n}\) with the horizontal lines \(y=1,\dots ,y=n-k\) and the upper part with the \(k\) sunny lines (translated upward). Hence it suffices to decide for which \(k\) the set \(S_{k}\) can be covered by \(k\) sunny lines.

5.  Show that \(k=3\) is possible by the explicit three sunny lines  

    \[
    \begin{aligned}
    L_{1}&:\;y=x      &&\text{(through }(1,1),(2,2)),\\
    L_{2}&:\;y-3=-2(x-1) &&\text{(through }(1,3),(2,1)),\\
    L_{3}&:\;y-2=\tfrac12(x-1) &&\text{(through }(1,2),(3,1)).
    \end{aligned}
    \]

    These three lines cover all six points of \(S_{3}\).

6.  Prove that for every \(k\ge 4\) a covering of \(S_{k}\) by \(k\) sunny lines is impossible.  
    *   Each side of the right‑angled triangle \(S_{k}\) contains exactly \(k\) lattice points:
        \[
        \begin{aligned}
        C&=\{(1,t)\mid 1\le t\le k\},\\
        R&=\{(s,1)\mid 1\le s\le k\},\\
        H&=\{(i,k+1-i)\mid 1\le i\le k\}.
        \end{aligned}
        \]
    *   A sunny line cannot be parallel to any side, therefore it meets each side in **at most one** point.
    *   With \(k\) sunny lines we can meet each side in at most \(k\) points, so every line must meet **exactly one** point of each side.
    *   Consequently each line would contain three points, one from each side.  
        However three points taken from the three distinct sides of a right‑angled triangle are never collinear unless two of them are vertices of the triangle.  
        The only possible collinear triples are  
        \((1,k),(k,1),(1,1)\); any line containing two of these vertices has slope \(0,\infty\) or \(-1\), i.e. it is non‑sunny – a contradiction.
    *   Hence no family of \(k\) sunny lines can cover all points of \(S_{k}\) when \(k\ge 4\).

7.  Combining the above, the only values of \(k\) for which a configuration exists are \(k=0,1,3\).  

**Detailed Solution**

Let  

\[
S_{n}= \{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{2}\mid a+b\le n+1\}.
\]

A line is *sunny* iff its slope is different from \(0\), \(\infty\) and \(-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Constructions for \(k=0\) and \(k=1\)

* \(k=0\): the \(n\) horizontal lines  

  \[
  y=1,\;y=2,\dots ,y=n
  \]

  are distinct, non‑sunny and each point of \(S_{n}\) lies on exactly one of them.

* \(k=1\): use the \(n-1\) horizontal lines  

  \[
  y=1,\;y=2,\dots ,y=n-1
  \]

  which cover all points of \(S_{n}\) except \((1,n)\).  
  The line  

  \[
  L:\;y-n = x-1\qquad(\text{slope }1)
  \]

  passes through \((1,n)\) and is sunny.  Thus a configuration with exactly one sunny line exists for every \(n\ge3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Impossibility of \(k=2\)

Assume a configuration with exactly two sunny lines exists.  
Take the \(n-2\) non‑sunny lines to be the horizontal lines  

\[
y=1,\;y=2,\dots ,y=n-2 .
\]

All points of \(S_{n}\) with second coordinate \(\le n-2\) are already covered.  
The three points  

\[
A=(1,n),\qquad B=(1,n-1),\qquad C=(2,n-1)
\]

remain uncovered.  

Any line through two of \(A,B,C\) has slope \(0\) (horizontal), \(\infty\) (vertical) or \(-1\) (parallel to \(x+y=0\); indeed \(\overline{AC}\) has slope \(-1\)).  
Hence a sunny line can contain **at most one** of the three points.  
With only two sunny lines at least one of \(A,B,C\) stays uncovered – a contradiction.  
Therefore \(k=2\) is impossible for every \(n\ge3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Reduction to the triangle \(S_{k}\)

Suppose we have a configuration for some \(n\) with exactly \(k\) sunny lines (\(k\ge3\)).  
Remove the \(n-k\) horizontal lines \(y=1,\dots ,y=n-k\).  
The points that are still uncovered are precisely  

\[
U_{k}= \{(a,b)\in S_{n}\mid b\ge n-k+1\}.
\]

If we translate the coordinates by the vector \((0,n-k)\) (i.e. replace \((a,b)\) by \((a,b-(n-k))\)), the set \(U_{k}\) becomes  

\[
S_{k}= \{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^{2}\mid a+b\le k+1\}.
\]

Thus a configuration for \((n,k)\) exists **iff** the triangle \(S_{k}\) can be covered by exactly \(k\) sunny lines.  
Consequently we only have to decide for which integers \(k\ge3\) the set \(S_{k}\) admits such a covering.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  A covering for \(k=3\)

The three sunny lines  

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{1}&:\;y=x,\\
L_{2}&:\;y-3=-2(x-1),\\
L_{3}&:\;y-2=\tfrac12(x-1)
\end{aligned}
\]

have slopes \(1,-2,\tfrac12\), none of which is \(0,\infty,-1\).  
Their integer points are

\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{1}&:\;(1,1),(2,2),\\
L_{2}&:\;(1,3),(2,1),\\
L_{3}&:\;(1,2),(3,1).
\end{aligned}
\]

These six points are exactly the elements of \(S_{3}\).  
Hence \(k=3\) is attainable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Impossibility of \(k\ge4\)

Let \(k\ge4\) and assume that \(k\) sunny lines cover all points of \(S_{k}\).  
Denote the three sides of the right‑angled triangle \(S_{k}\) by  

\[
\begin{aligned}
C&=\{(1,t)\mid 1\le t\le k\}\quad\text{(the left side)},\\
R&=\{(s,1)\mid 1\le s\le k\}\quad\text{(the bottom side)},\\
H&=\{(i,k+1-i)\mid 1\le i\le k\}\quad\text{(the hypotenuse)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Each side contains exactly \(k\) lattice points.

*Because a sunny line is not parallel to any of the three sides, it can meet each side in at most one point.*  
Hence a sunny line can contain **at most three** points of \(S_{k}\), one from each side.

Since there are \(k\) points on each side and only \(k\) lines, every line must meet **exactly one** point of each side; otherwise some side would have fewer than \(k\) intersection points, contradicting the fact that all its points must be covered.

Consequently each of the \(k\) lines contains a triple  

\[
\bigl(1,t_i\bigr),\qquad\bigl(s_i,1\bigr),\qquad\bigl(i,k+1-i\bigr)
\]

with \(t_i,s_i,i\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\).  
These three points are collinear.

However three points taken from the three distinct sides of a right‑angled triangle are never collinear, except when two of them are vertices of the triangle.  
The only possible collinear triples are

\[
(1,k),\;(k,1),\;(1,1),
\]

but any line containing two of these vertices has slope \(0\) (horizontal), \(\infty\) (vertical) or \(-1\) (the hypotenuse), i.e. it is **non‑sunny**.  
Thus a sunny line cannot contain a collinear triple of the required form, a contradiction.

Therefore no family of \(k\) sunny lines can cover all points of \(S_{k}\) when \(k\ge4\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion

*   \(k=0\) and \(k=1\) are always realizable (Section 1).
*   \(k=2\) is never realizable (Section 2).
*   \(k=3\) is realizable (Section 4).
*   No \(k\ge4\) is realizable (Section 5).

Hence for every integer \(n\ge3\) the set of admissible numbers of sunny lines is exactly  

\[
\boxed{\{0,1,3\}} .
\]
